utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am Eric Ostberg. I appear this session with Mr. Giuliano Turone and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. Ms. Teresa McHenry has other tasks this afternoon. Thank you. MSMr. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good afternoon. My name is Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me in the defence team is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor of Criminal Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic. I am defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Mr. Michael Greaves will not be with me in the courthouse this afternoon, so that I will be responsible for the cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honour. Tom Moran for Hazim Delic. My lead counsel, as the court is well aware, is out of town on other business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. I am John Ackerman appearing on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. Ms. McMurrey is in the United States for a court appearance that she is required to make there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now have the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to call Witness O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the witness. Let him take his oath. Witness O (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Because of the protection you have asked for and been granted I will in this courtroom address you with the pseudonym O; is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Sir, due to what you are going to testify to in this trial we cannot possibly conceal your profession. Would you mind telling us what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is no secret. I am by profession a surgeon, a trauma surgeon and orthopaedic surgeon and I can speak about my profession and I hope what I say will be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I will address you as Dr O in our conversation. Can you tell the court what kind of speciality, if any, you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I first graduated medical school. Then I specialised in general surgery and after that traumatology and orthopaedics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Considering the fact that many doctors practise in the city where you practise, would it be in any way harmful to you if you told us where you practise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am working in a clinical centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It appears from the investigation made by the Prosecution's office that you have examined at least 24 persons who have been previously detained in the Celebici camp in Konjic. Can you, without revealing your identity, tell us how that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually in Konjic, and the detainees upon leaving the camp all knew of me, and sought medical assistance from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When I asked you how it happened, I also meant if you could tell the court where they came to see you and how they announced their coming. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since I am working at this large clinical centre in Belgrade, upon being released from the camp they had heard of me and they came in groups as they left the camp, but some of those people knew me from before, and that is why they came, and they passed on to others that they would be given medical treatment by me, and that is why quite a large number of the people released from the camp looked me up for me to examine them and extend medical aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did they make a previous appointment with your sector nurse, or did they just show up at your clinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't make appointments with my secretary. They just came individually when they left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. Was it correctly stated that -- I mentioned the figure 24. Is that a correct figure of people who had been detained in Celebici camp that you examined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is not the exact figure. There were more of them that came. I brought with me the documentation for the 24. I could have brought more if the court so requires. I can bring more, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but we have this 24. I now ask my case manager to give the originals of your statements to the Registrar to be marked for identification, and then I will show them to Dr O one by one in the order they are put. The defence have been provided with copies of these statements and they appear in Serbo-Croatian and also appear in English translation. The court is now also given copies in English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. Are they planning on introducing this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We are trying to introduce these things as evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have a few objections before it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could we have our witness -- could we have them marked and have our witness look at them before your objections are raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine. I just have some objections on several things as to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. What I will try to do now, Dr O, is to go through with you the 24 statements, and you will tell the court whether you have made the statements and signed the statements and seen the patient in question. I will start with a patient by the name of Novica Kuljanin. Do you have them before you or are you still waiting for them? . We are still waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I ask the Tribunal's patience while they are being marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my understanding that what Mr. Ostberg is asking now is merely identification and that there will be no testimony about what is contained in the document by this witness. With that understanding I have no problem with him going ahead with the identification, but if he plans to get into any of the content of any of these statements, then Mr. Moran and I, I think, both have objections in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he will first identify them as documents coming from his jurisdiction. Later if there is any need for going further ....

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can we do it this way, Dr O? We start with number one in the English translation. The patient is Novica Kuljanin. Did you examine him and sign a statement concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number two is a patient by the name of Ranko Ninkovic. Did you examine and sign a statement concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number three is Slobodan Zelenovic. Same statement concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number four, Radovan Mrsic. Same question concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number five is Radoslav Vujicic. Same question concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Six is Vukasin Mrkajic. Same questions concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The seventh is Goran Djure Gligorevic. Same question concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number eight is Sreten Zelenovic. Same question concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: My number nine is Dragan Kuljanin. Same questions concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number ten is Ranko Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 11 is Simo Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number 12 is Sretko Sinikovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I apologise whenever I try to pronounce these names. I do my best. Number 13 is Miodrag Inujundzic. Is that yes also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number 14 is Novica Ivkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. 15 is Branislav Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 16 is Dragan Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 17 is Zeljko Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 18 is Branislav Gligorevic; is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 19 is Jelenko Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number 20 is Duro Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You find that also. Number 21 is Janko Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number 22 is Nenad Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Number 23 is Bosko Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Fine. The last one is Radoslav Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr O?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What I would like to do now, your Honours, is to go to the content of these statements and ask Dr O whether he had made the findings in the document before signing it. That will be my next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just a moment. There is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would lodge an objection to any testimony from this witness regarding the contents of this document. The court has it before it. You can look at each of these documents. It is clear that in each of these documents what is contained there is a medical diagnosis as a result of a medical examination, where medical findings were found. This witness will, if discussing what is contained in these documents, be testifying as an expert witness. He will be giving his opinions as an expert, not observations that he made as a lay person. There is an order entered by this court regarding notification to us by the Prosecutor of who will be their expert witnesses. This particular witness was never -- there was never any notification to the defence pursuant to the order of this court in the terms of the order of this court that this witness would be called as an expert witness. We, therefore, have not had the opportunity that we would have had if we had received notification timely and in accordance with that order to do the investigations and to do the research that would be necessary to properly cross-examine an expert witness on these matters. Therefore, we object to this witness referring to the contents of these documents. We object to the admission of the documents, and we object to any testimony by this witness that would be in the nature of expert testimony, that is an opinion based upon a medical examination, a finding based upon a medical examination that he did of any of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to add to that objection, even if he is allowed to testify as an expert, these documents are full of things that are clearly outside of his expertise as a physician. Specifically let us just pick one at random from the middle of the document. Dragan Mrkajic. I do not even know what number he is but the first phrase in here is: "Patient released from the Ustasha detention camp from Celebici in Konjic". That is clearly outside any knowledge any physician would have as an expert. He clearly has no personal knowledge about any of that. It is well outside of any expert testimony that he could give.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. May I deal with this last objection first and say this is certainly why he is called as a mixed witness by the Prosecution. This is a fact I am going to question him about, and I maintain that this is saying what the patient told him, namely where he came from, is hearsay. I think the learned counsel agrees that that is hearsay, but my point is that this is admissible hearsay, because it has probative value and it is reliable and, in my view, even if I am not an expert in common law, which I have had the opportunity to demonstrate many times, even in that jurisdiction I believe hearsay consisting of information from a doctor of what -- not being a doctor-client privileged -- what a patient told him under asking for advice or treatment would be admissible under the presumption that the circumstances are such that it must be considered reliable. Therefore, in so far what Dr O can tell us is to be considered hearsay, it is admissible hearsay, and it is reliable hearsay. It has probative value and there is no prejudice against any defendant in the evidence of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, along that line, the first thing is I do not think hearsay is a rule. If Mr. Ostberg wants to debate the contents of the Federal Rule of evidence 8035, I will be happy to do it with him. The fact of the matter is the Tadic Rule is what applies in this court. Tadic says it has to be reliable and has to be reliable as a statement made from medical diagnosis or treatment. The statement would have to relate to medical diagnosis or treatment. The fact that someone has injured -- in fact, it is an a written motion I handed to the court some time ago. While it may very well be a statement that: "I was hit by a car" may be a medical diagnosis or treatment, but the fact it was a yellow car at the corner of 5th Avenue and Madison Avenue in New York City is not medical diagnosis or treatment. It is outside of that kind of reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, all these persons he examined, are they witnesses before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All these persons the doctor has examined are witnesses before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Not all. Some are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe the statement they were detained in Ustasha camp would not be such a reliable piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I did not quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Rule of hearsay admits only reliable evidence which goes to value. Persons who are not witnesses before us, somebody has said that to him. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This court has already ruled that even things happen to persons not being mentioned in the indictment, for instance, can be heard, due to the fact they are general allegations of creating conditions in this camp. I would like to relate this to the counts 38, 39, 46, 47. Through this I am going to substantiate that these people were in Celebici camp. Your Honour is now referring to a name on the camp, and only Dr O can tell us why he put that down and how he got it. I am going to -- I bring this witness for the very simple reason to show the court these people we have now heard the name of have all been detained as prisoners in Celebici, and this is the fact that these people were brought to the witness I am going to examine. This witness happened to be a doctor and happened to be in the position to have diagnosed and helped these people. So that is why he is a mixed witness, and I think that his statement is to me clearly admissible. I cannot see -- as I just said about hearsay, it is hearsay. When a patient comes into this doctor's office and says: "I am detained in Celebici camp for three months and I had this and this illness as a result of it", could that not be a fact that a witness could give to the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the main contention is not that he cannot give evidence but he might not be able to give evidence in a particular capacity, that is as an expert on the matters which he intends to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: To come over that hurdle, your Honour, we have sent the defence lawyers his CV and they can clearly see that he is a doctor with a certain speciality and fully capable of establishing through examination the status of a patient. That is all I want to bring him for. We have tried to get over that by giving the CV. He is in that capacity an expert. I have before me, if I will go on arguing, the Modern Law of Evidence, Adrian Keane. On page 378 -- the title is the Modern Law of Evidence -- saying: "A non-expert witness", as we have seen, "may give opinion evidence on matters in relation to which it is impossible or virtually impossible to separate his inferences from the perceived facts on which those inferences are based. In this circumstance the witness is permitted to express his opinion as a compendious means of conveying to the court the facts he perceived".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, a lay opinion would be something like: "He smelled of alcohol. He was stumbling. In my opinion he was drunk." That is a lay opinion. The fact that a man's left rib has been healing and shown by X-rays or that he has strong palpitatory soreness on the left side of the left haemothorax sounds to me a whole lot like something that would go beyond a lay opinion and would require some sort of special training and expertise such as medical school. Also we were, in fact, provided with a one-page resume on May 26th. That is the date of the cover letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have also heard the witness himself. The witness has given you his credentials too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually, your Honour, I am not sure he has. It does not show anything about any residency. It does not show anything at all about any undergraduate study. It does not show anything about any internship, any articles that this person may or may not have published. Those are the kinds of things that at least I would consider important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Here before us he has told us he attended medical school, he graduated in general surgery, traumatology and orthopaedic surgery. At least we have heard that here. I know no notification of the matter has been given to you earlier for you to pursue it, but at least you know the area of his specialisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you given a copy of this document to the defence earlier or are you producing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: They have had it long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have had it for -- I was handed this document in English the last time this witness was supposed to testify, that day or the day before, so whenever that was. Because of the delays we have had, it is -- I have had it a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is not the whole truth, as far as I can hear, because we have given the translations long beforehand to all the defence, that this was a revisited -- it was brought to my attention that this was not in some parts absolutely accurate. Then as a service to the defence lawyers we gave them a revised one in its totality a document like the other one they already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The original one I had had five names on it that were contained somewhere in these nails. I understand it was provided some time ago in Bosnian, but the 24 names, the first I saw of them was some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your objection is mainly you have not been able to verify the claims of his qualification. Is that your main objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. First, he has not been designated. Secondly, he is clearly testifying as an expert. At least from this document he is clearly going to be testifying -- at least they want him to testify outside his area of expertise to some extent, and finally these documents refer to a lot of things that because we have not been provided with the full copy of the report, we cannot verify. For example, numerous, the very first page, says X-rays enclosed. The very top one, Novica Kuljanin. If there is an X-ray enclosed, I cannot get a copy of that X-ray and send it to an orthopaedic surgeon somewhere else and say: "Okay, doctor. What does that X-ray show?" . The third one, Zelenovic: "X-ray of the chest shows". Fourth one, Mrsic, however that is pronounced, X-ray of the thorax. Next page, two X-rays. One below that, Mrkajic, Vukasin Mrkajic, X-ray. Next page, Gligorevic, X-ray. Zelenovic, x-ray of the chest. Just to give the Trial Chamber some example. How can I have someone else -- I do not have the expertise to look at an X-ray and say this shows a compression fracture of L5. I would have to hire that gun. I would have to have that X-ray go to somebody. That is why in January the Trial Chamber entered an order about expert witnesses, designations, CVs, set deadlines. That is why it was done. If this man wants to give what would be a lay opinion, I have no problem with that. If he has some personal knowledge about what he saw at Celebici, what he saw in the Konjic area, what he saw in areas relevant to this case, I have no problem with him testifying about that. If he wants to come in and say someone was limping, one of these people was limping, that is a lay opinion. I have no problem with him testifying about that, but when you start getting beyond that, you start getting into the area of true expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, I cannot accept this objection that this is not -- everything has not been brought to the attention of the defence counsel. Mr. Karabdic inspected the Serbo-Croatian originals in July 1996. I cannot help that counsel are partly speaking Serbo-Croat and partly speaking English. I can do nothing about the communication between counsel of different languages, but proper counsel for all defendants has been given this in July or June 1996, every single statement contended now in translation before the learned judges. That is reality. If you have miscommunication, that is not to be a burden on the shoulders of the prosecution, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two matters that I would like to address regarding this. The first one is a pure evidentiary question. I happen to be, not to be self-aggrandising, the author of a treatise on Law of Evidence that is widely used in Texas. When we talk about the hearsay rule and the exceptions that have grown up with regard to the hearsay rule in that system, the exceptions are all based upon what a court there would call circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness. There can be an exception to hearsay if there can be a determination that that statement is trustworthy or reliable, as the Tadic Decision would instruct. Therefore, statements made to a doctor for purposes of treatment are generally considered to be reliable, because a person is there wanting to make sure that the doctor has sufficient information so that a proper treatment decision and diagnosis can be made. A statement like: "I was in Ustasha camp in Celebici" has nothing to do with the diagnosis of any condition that person may present or the treatment which may need to be prescribed for that treatment (sic), so there is not any law which would support that particular statement coming under a reliability standard with regard to statements made for the purpose of diagnosis or treatment. Now, it may be, and I am not quite certain because Mr. Ostberg's representation was a bit ambiguous, it may be this witness is prepared to testify that he was at Celebici camp and saw all these people there. If that is true, then yes, he can say: "I saw this particular person when I visited Celebici camp." Then he can give evidence that that person was there. If some of these people are to be called as witnesses then, of course, they can tell the court they were in Celebici camp, but for anyone who is not going to be called here as a witness, for this witness to say: "I was told by my patient that he was in a camp in Celebici" is, I think, extremely unreliable and should not be accepted by this court. Now, the second matter: ordinarily, and I think without exception, when an expert witness is slated to testify in a case, the opponent of that evidence is entitled to all of the underlying data upon which that expert makes his expert conclusion. In this case that underlying data certainly consists of X-rays which have never been provided to us. In addition, that underlying data must of necessity consist of laboratory tests, because throughout these reports we see findings that the urine contained traces of blood. That is not a finding that can be made visually. That is a finding that has to be made in the laboratory. You cannot look at urine and say what it is that is discolouring that urine is blood. You may guess that, but you may not make that as a diagnosis without a laboratory analysis. So I am making the assumption that in each of these cases where there is a statement that there was blood in the urine that there was a laboratory test which confirms that. We have not been provided with any laboratory tests. So the problem with this witness not being designated properly as an expert and then coming here to give expert testimony is that we have not been provided with the underlying data upon which that testimony is based. Without that underlying data, we cannot show it to our own expert for the purpose of preparing a cross-examination or for the purpose of calling our own expert to counter what this one is saying. We have to take this person's word for what he saw on the X-ray. We have to take this person's word for what he read in a laboratory test. That is not the way it is supposed to work. That is not the way justice says it is supposed to work. Now, if the Prosecution wants to designate this person -- I mean, we were talking about this almost two weeks ago and they have still not designated him as an expert. They gave us a CV. The CV we have today does not seem to match the testimony he just gave here. The CV, your Honours, is in the English translation less than half a page. I am showing it to you (indicating). He told us today when he began that he had received specialised training in traumatology and orthopaedics. If we look at the CV that is given to us, there is nothing in here that says he has received that specialised training. There is simply a short statement at the bottom that says he is now practising as a specialist in traumatology and orthopaedics. I do not know if one practises in a clinic in Belgrade without special training in traumatology and orthopaedics or whether he has had special training in trauma and orthopaedics, or where he has had the special training in trauma and orthopaedics. I do not know what university we may contact to say was Dr O a student at that university. As far as we know, we have a person that has just walked in out of the ozone, representing himself to be a doctor, who now wants to testify as an expert before this court without having been designated as an expert by the Prosecution. I think this is highly irregular and highly improper. There may come a time, if we are furnished with the underlying data upon which this person's expertise is based, that the Prosecution could very well call him, because then we would be prepared to conduct the kind of cross-examination that would be necessary. We would be prepared to have our own experts look at the X-rays. We would be prepared to have our own experts look at the laboratory reports to see if they agree with him. They may very well agree with him but we are not ever going to know that until we see that underlying data and have an opportunity to examine it. What could easily happen and why the rules are the way they are and why we do things the way we do it, it could very easily happen that this person would come in here, give you his opinions without any of us receiving the underlying data and then find out six months from now, a year from now, two years from now, when someone may have the opportunity to look at the underlying data, that there is not any, that there are no X-rays, that the X-rays do not show what he claims them to show, that the laboratory tests do not say what he claims them to say. If we are going to have evidence before a court of this importance and a court upon which the eyes of the world are focused, then it ought to be done regularly and properly and in the way that justice demands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, have you any replies to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, I have the following. The simple fact is that 24 persons who had been detainees in the Celebici after being released go to see a doctor to have observation on what is the result of the mistreatment they have undergone and ask for advice to be sent on to other clinics and to get help. The Prosecution got the information of the existence of such a doctor. The Prosecution asked the doctor to provide us with the statements he has taken during looking at these patients. These we sent off to our defence lawyers, saying: "We are going to examine this doctor as a witness to establish what he learned from these persons and what he found on these persons". The position now, the reactions now made to all what we want to do, namely to examine this doctor and to listen to him, to hear him, answer questions on cross-examination and so on, to find out what did he really see, and I believe that this is exactly what we find in our statute, something of probative value. All these technical obstacles should be weighed against the weight this probative value would have. I reiterate myself in saying they are given to a doctor in the situation of patient-doctor. They are by their nature reliable. They stand the reliable test. They are probative and the weight of the evidence is to be found out by these learned trial judges. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: My understanding is that they are questioning your compliance with the rules about designation of an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. My answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Whether you have actually done so and what the effects will be on non-compliance with Rule 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Look at Rule 5 of our rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I know, your Honour. Putting him on the list, I saw him as a mixed witness to facts and being an expert, and I tried to combine these two and combined it with what my experience of matters like this in my former practice in the Scandinavian countries and found this was a proper way of doing it. Maybe I therefore did not follow this expertise Rule. The word was "expert" in the list of witnesses, that he was an expert as a doctor, but the formal way, as your Honours are now -- indicates, may not have been followed. That is true. I tried to re-do that in a way by supporting his statements to them in very due time and then to support my opponents with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Try and look up Rule 5 of our rules about the effect of non-compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, I have read this, your Honour. My answer to it is these objections have not been raised at the earliest opportunity. I cannot find it affects any principles of fairness or has occasioned miscarriage of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What does Ustasha mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have no translation to it. I know it is used as a degrading name on warriors from the former Yugoslavia. It is for our witness to explain why this expression appears in a statement. I cannot give any explanation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge Jan, maybe I can help you with that. Ustasha were Croats who were members of a political party during the Second World War who were very closely allied with the German occupiers of the former Yugoslavia. They have a reputation -- would this be fair -- of being very closely allied with the Nazis -- is that a fair assessment -- during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought Ustasha was a court organisation, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. As I recall, it was a political party that was again -- it is a pejorative term. It is a very pejorative term, your Honour, in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Linked to violence, linked to violence, but I cannot give any explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you wish to make any contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I fully agree with my colleagues. I would just like to clarify this element of complete lack of the ontology and the rules of medicine. It is obvious from the case histories in these papers here. It is obvious (redacted) not take the personal details of the persons who were examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have to redact something at this point. There was a name mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us explain to Mr. Olujic. I think you do not mention the names. The witness here is known as Dr O. That is all we refer to in here

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. So there are no personal details here of birth next to the patient's name. For instance, patient number 1 could have been born last year, five days ago or 80 years ago. Second point, it is absolutely impossible that the witnesses, that all the victims, patients described here who went to see Dr O, it is impossible that all of them could have said that they had come from Ustasha camp. It is completely impossible. Anyone who is familiar with the situation in former Yugoslavia is, of course, aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will rise for a few minutes and make a ruling when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has considered the matter very carefully and we think we would allow Dr O to give evidence, but subject to certain safeguards and conditions. The Prosecution must supply the defence with all the particular annexures, X-rays and all the tests in which you were involved in the reports. They also must give the complete curriculum vitae of Dr O and would postpone cross-examination on Dr O when the defence has verified these things, because the defence might not be able to go into full cross-examination of these things when all these facts are lacking, but Dr O can give his evidence now, but subject to the objections of the defence. That is the decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that happens, is it possible that I may enquire of the witness one or two questions just to make certain that what the Trial Chamber has just ordered is a possible accomplishment? That is are the X-rays and the lab tests even available any more, or ask Mr. Ostberg to make -- to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Definitely that will be very relevant for any of those steps, if they want those documents admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If they are not available any more, it is impossible for the court to order them for handed over and makes it impossible for us to do a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This will be our first question to establish this fact. Dr O, in your statements you have, as already indicated by some of the defence lawyers, said that you took X-rays and you took blood tests and other laboratory tests. Are the documentation of these undertakings from your side available and can they be produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each finding referring to X-ray and laboratory tests, which is normal for examinations of this kind, because I am not a layman, as the defence counsel has said, but I cannot only distinguish whether a patient is limping on his right or left leg -- my grandmother can ascertain that. Therefore, there is the documentation, but each of those patients has that documentation. Wherever an X-ray is mentioned and the MG, of course defence counsel does not understand what that is, because he is not a doctor, just as I am not an attorney and that is why I cannot interfere. MG is a special test or finding --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can we stick to the X-rays first. If X-rays are taken, do you attach that to a file for these patients and keep it in your clinic? I did not quite understand what you said. Did you give the X-rays out to the patient to take it away with him, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us get our bearing. Are the results of these tests and X-rays available? That is the thing the defence wants to know, whether they are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are they available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those X-rays are in the hands of the patients as well as the laboratory's test findings as well as all other tests, because I am not able to keep the files on patients who are not regular patients of my clinic and to keep them in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would the answer then be that they are not available to you? Would the answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They are not available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is the answer, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the Ruling that was just handed down not two minutes ago, we object to any expert testimony from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think your Honours are also fully aware that what has just been testified to is highly irregular. I have never, ever, ever known of a doctor that did not keep X-rays, laboratory tests, things of that nature in his office. He turned them over to the patient. I mean, that is just highly irregular and very suspicious to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am sure that is not unusual, especially if the doctor has no X-ray unit. If his medical centre has no X-ray unit and they might have got the X-ray done elsewhere, he did not have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The answer is given, your Honour. This is not available to the doctor. I cannot stand up here and say that I can collect all these from these patients. I have no way to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is very difficult for them to cross-check whether, in fact, any X-ray was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That should go to the possibility then we have before we finish that I have to go through these 24 and see how many patients from whom X-rays were taken. There may be others that they did not take X-rays from others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Not just on X-rays. Blood tests and the samples, all these are relevant for the purposes of admitting the opinions of the tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I put in answer if it goes -- I am not quite in the clear. May I ask you, Dr O, your answer, does that go also to blood tests and other results taken outside your own clinic? You said that you do not have the X-rays. You gave them to the patient. Does that go also for blood tests and other laboratory results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I try to make myself clear. All results of tests are given to the patients because they wanted those tests, as many of them went to the States, Canada, other west European countries, and they took those results with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What I would ask for, your Honour, is a few minutes to run through this and see if there are statements left that might depend on other examinations than Dr O did himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Our problem is he would be testifying on things on which he cannot be examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, the defence is entitled to see the data upon which the expert has based his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. What I am hinting at is the possibility that there are some statements which are not based on anything but an examination in the examination room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Such as -- which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Such as palpitations, listening to the heart, seeing the patient, looking at scars and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That will not be expert evidence, because he is seeing what he has --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What he is seeing actually.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He will be giving evidence about what he actually saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He might have been examined. I cannot say on this without going through the 24 cases. He examined someone without having any extra means like blood tests or laboratory tests or X-rays. That is what I want to come to. Then I think it is in the ambit of the Ruling of the Trial Chamber that he can give evidence to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now let him proceed with whatever you can get him to say, because with the objections still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have them in mind, your Honour. Let us start with if you have before you the statement you wrote concerning Novica Kuljanin. Do you have it? You will get it from the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to save Mr. Ostberg some time, I have been through these and every one of them shows either an X-ray or a lab test of some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It says: "He complains of pains all over his body and his left arm in particular .... signs of lesion of mediamus and ulnaris with slight contracture of fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then, your Honour, it says: "X-ray is enclosed."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Therefore, your Honour, it is impossible to tell whether that is based upon what he saw in the X-ray or what he saw with his eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He complains of pains all over his body and his left arm. That has nothing to do with the X-ray.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is for sure. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We were allowed to continue and I will put my questions in a way that has nothing to do with this extra laboratory or extra tests. Then we have -- what I will ask to do, Dr O, is to tell you what your diagnosis is. It is in Latin and some of the defence lawyers have complained that they do not read Latin. Could you please tell us what the diagnosis is on Novica Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is what we have just been through. He was now asking what his diagnosis is which has to be based on lab tests and X-rays. You have already said, your Honours, that that cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We cannot make such an assessment until we have heard his diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, strictly speaking, all these tests could not be admitted until after cross-examination and you can verify it to be consistent with the examination. He will just give his evidence and then you would challenge it from all he has been asked. If he is unable to supply you with the facts, then that evidence cannot be substantiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand, your Honour, the Ruling. It is my understanding that we are not to cross-examine until the Prosecutor has supplied us with whatever X-rays and lab tests that can be found. It seems to me until we know what X-rays and lab tests can be found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Until you are able to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand, but it seems to me until we know that this person's testimony should not be given, because then you will be hearing testimony that we are incapable of cross-examining because we do not have those things. Now, I understand that what Mr. Ostberg proposes to do now is have the witness sit here and say: "Patient Kuljanin said he had pains all over his body and his left arm in particular." I'm not sure that gets us anywhere other than just wasting some time. It seems to me the thing to do is thank this witness for coming, let Mr. Ostberg and the Prosecution gather up however many X-rays and lab tests they can gather up and get them to us. Once we have had them for a reasonable amount of time, then bring the witness back and testify about those particular patients upon which we can reasonably conduct a cross-examination, but the way this has just started out after the court's Ruling: "What is your diagnosis?" , the diagnosis depends upon the X-rays and the lab tests. That is not a proper question. Maybe a proper question, if the court wants to hear something from this witness today, is: "What did the patient tell you about his symptoms?" , not going into, I hope, the Ustasha camp in Celebici part, because I think that is not admissible in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually your position is a very difficult one, because in order to support any of the things being put forward here you must have the supporting data. You do not appear to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I do not have them and I cannot promise even to be successful in gathering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: In any case he cannot give evidence of what is in here. He cannot give evidence of what is stated in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If the ruling is that is not possible without this background material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No evidence is complete except after cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We merely wanted to give opportunity to test the veracity of those things, if, in fact, they do exist. If they do not exist there is nothing on which they can be tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see how you can continue when you are quite sure that there are no other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just a second for consultation. (Pause.) What I can do, your Honours, is, as far as I can see, only to question the witness on what -- on the meeting with the patient in question, what he could see on the patients in question without relying on this background tests that has been contested, and even I find the ruling encompassed the possibility for me to ask the question: "What is the meaning of the Ustasha detention camp?", etc. I rely again on this case law which I brought forward that a non-expert witness and mixed witness can rely on his expertise. He cannot separate these two issues from each other. He can say: "This patient came into my office. He told me what he has sustained and what is his symptoms and then was given advice." I would stay away from any questions pertaining to the results based on -- diagnosis based on X-rays or blood tests, etc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, one of the objections is his credentials as a surgeon, as a doctor. That is even doubted. They do not have the particulars to cross-check what is being claimed. Whatever your views are, they are entitled to know and they deserve to see those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In that I think the witness himself can remedy that in examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure how that is going to help you. We have evidence that detainees were beaten before they reached Celebici camp mercilessly at the time of their arrest and much time has elapsed between their release from the camp and their examination. So one does not know at what stage they received these injuries. We are more concerned with what happened inside the Celebici camp. So I do not know how this is going to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. In my legal system this witness would be called a support witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A support witness. The support must be indicated towards the main evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Linked to the place, linked to what happened, linked to the counts in the indictment, etc, but a support witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I asked you right in the beginning are these witnesses going to appear before us and you said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I did not say no. I said some are. Some have and some are to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Confine yourself to those persons whose evidence you want to support instead of taking all this. Refer to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I can do that, but then I have to go into closed session, because these witnesses, I think all of them are protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I can do that in closed session, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then in that case it will be supporting evidence, but I do not know if the main evidence is not there, what are you going to support?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We are thinking about five persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can do it in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then I will have to ask your Honours to let me go into closed session, because these witnesses have been given protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Even if this is supported evidence, it still has to be based on something. The fact that I presume this man can testify that witness whoever came in and had a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, if there is evidence of a person saying that he was maltreated inside the Celebici camp, the doctor can come and say: "Yes, he came to me and he was complaining of all these injuries he received." That probably would be supporting evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think he can probably testify that far. I do not think he can say "so and so said he was in Celebici camp and this, that and the other." He can say: "The guy came in and had a black eye", that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think that will also be supporting evidence. He goes to his doctor and says he was in that camp. That would probably be admissible to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Well, I would confine myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Right in the beginning I asked Mr. Ostberg if any of these persons was appearing as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think I count five on his witness list. By the way, noone has ever said that someone who said he was in Celebici camp was not there. That has never been an issue before the court. So I do not know how relevant that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If we go into closed session, I will confine myself to put questions about these five persons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we now come down to an issue of what is really the best way to proceed at this point. It looks to me like where we are going now is that we are going to take a little bit of testimony from this witness at this point, which will not be cross-examined, and then bring him back at some future date and take more direct testimony from him, which then would be subject to examination, and we were talking about dribs and drabs yesterday. It may not make sense to present testimony in that kind of a drib and drab way. It is also not real late in the day but it is somewhat late in the day. It seems to me what makes sense both for the expediency of this court and for the continuity of what we are doing here that we simply excuse the witness at this point until the matter of what is available in terms of tests and X-rays has been resolved. He is obviously going to have to come back anyhow. At that point it can all be done in one whole part rather than the dribs and drabs that we seem to be moving into at this point. That is just a suggestion. It is not an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a fair suggestion, because initially we thought perhaps these materials providing the data might be found, so that it makes it easier for the defence to determine how to tackle the cross-examination, but if they are not there at all, I begin to wonder the wisdom of even postponing, because if they are not there at all, whether you postpone or not, you still would not find them: I do not know what he was coming to do when he knew those things were not part of the evidence he was coming to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is true. (Pause). Your Honours, in the circumstances what I have left to do is treat him exactly as a fact witness and just ask him of the visits of these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And you will forget him as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then I forget him as an expert witness. I use him as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then, Dr O, maybe we can have some answers and the answers would be of not the kind of your examination of these patients that visited you, but to the fact if and when they came to you. I start again with Novica Kuljanin. Do you remember this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Novica Kuljanin just by his diagnosis that I wrote down. As far as this specific case is concerned in order to show what the situation was really like to the Trial Chamber, no X-rays were made in the case of Kuljanin nor lab tests, except for the MG. This is the kind of test which I already explained what kind it was. As for the diagnosis, he had a gunshot wound to his left --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just a moment. We should, due to the ruling of the court, stick to the fact of the visit of him. My question is: what do you remember of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to keep rising and objecting. I had understood that we had at least gotten to the point where the Chamber had taken the position that those who were not to be called as witnesses here, that as to those persons this was not supporting evidence, and now we are going there, and maybe that is the wish of the Trial Chamber. I do not know, but I had the impression, maybe the wrong one, that we were only then to talk about the five who were going to be called here as witnesses on that kind of a basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No. I did not understand it that way. As the fact witness, he can tell about every person coming and telling where he had been and why he came to him, the pure fact. That can be made, in my opinion, by every one of them as evidence to the counts against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, your Honours, my earlier suggestion still makes a great deal of sense. I think in order to accomplish this without an objection every few seconds, the Prosecutor at least needs to reinstruct his witness as to where the testimony is going at this point. The witness still seems to think he is here to testify as an expert, and clearly he is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic? MSMr. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I fully agree with my colleague Ackerman, because in the answer to the first question made by the Prosecutor the answer is the only kind that this witness can actually give, and he said that he knows Novica Kuljanin just by the diagnosis that he himself gave. Thus he goes back to his expert knowledge and expert explanation. Over three or four years it is absolutely normal that this witness cannot testify as to how this person came into his clinic and what he looked like. So I think that we are really in a situation now that we are facing a fact that has to be resolved just as my colleague suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will disagree to an extent with my two colleagues over here, my two friends. I think that Dr O said something about this man had a gunshot wound. I think that a lot of people other than physicians can recognise a gunshot wound. If somebody comes in with a bullet in his belly, I think we know that if it is still bleeding and still there, most people or many people could recognise that as a gunshot wound, but the other side of the coin is if it would have been a gunshot wound that was healed six months or a year ago, that might require special expertise and he may not be able to testify about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will rise until about 5 o'clock and allow Mr. Ostberg to organise himself and know the limits within which the defects in the witness' ability to testify and allow him to lead any evidence. If he is unable to do so, he will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHITE
utterances.text: We spent very valuable time getting you to sort your matters out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I do appreciate that recess to enable me to do so. I know exactly what I am trying to do. I am now treating Dr O as a fact witness and I will put a very few questions to him, and my aim with these is to tender these statements for the purpose which I will end up telling you. I will now ask you, Dr O, you have already testified that you signed these statements. Are these records kept in your normal course of business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your answer to my question was yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Do these records accurately reflect the names of the persons that came to you for treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly they indicate the names of the people who came to me seeking assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do these statements accurately reflect what the patients told you in seeking treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. May I just make a point of clarification, because the question was asked why the words "Ustasha camp" is stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You do not have to elaborate on that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out what the word "Ustasha" meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You wanted an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I got the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you carry on, you have other statements other than the documents you tendered to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: They are what you are referring to now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What you have before you is what I am referring to now. I will conclude by telling you what I am going to do with them but on the way to reach this point I ask now: can you please tell this court what is Ustasha and clarify to us all what is meant when the word "Ustasha" appears in the papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not make up this word. This is a word that exists for a long time, but when a patient comes to see a doctor, the initial contact is established through conversation. Then you ask him how he feels, what he has come, where he has come from. All of them stated that they came from an Ustasha camp. That is their statement, because, you know, there is first the history of the disease. You have to find out how the disease developed. Then comes the clinical examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is outside the question. All we want to know is what is the meaning of that expression, Ustasha camp. That is all we want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That can easily be translated. It means a criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Back to your statements. Do these statements accurately reflect what the patients told you in seeking treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course they do reflect everything the patients said, and that is what I put down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is as far as I want to go in bringing this fact witness. I now want to tender these statements for the sole purpose of showing the identity of these concerned persons who came to Dr O's office and to show what they reported to him, and I stay away from all the medical statements made in the statements and want to introduce them just for these two purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, they should be read out orally. The statements should be read to show exactly what they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. I could also. He has testified that he has signed them and that the person has been there, but if to reach my goal your Honours want it to be read out, I am perfectly happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Surely, because if you are setting claims that this is what the documents themselves contain, you must establish those claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, and then again I see three gentlemen standing up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In that I stick only to what they told the doctor, not the doctor's finding, not the doctor's diagnosis, not the doctor's, whatever he did. Just I give you the doctor's business record for all that it is worth. I will read them and read exactly what they stated when they came into his office without going into his findings as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have got an objection for starters that he is trying to get these things introduced as a business record. To be a business record, the very first thing is it has to be kept in the normal course of business. I would suggest these things were prepared in contemplation of litigation, ie so it was not kept in the normal course of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He has asked my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The second thing is you still have to get by the reliability portion that we have testified about. We talked about earlier that to be reliable, to be admissible under Tadic, as something -- as a statement made for medical diagnosis and treatment, it has to be directly related to the medical diagnosis and treatment. The fact that this person came from a Ustasha camp is clearly not made for medical diagnosis for treatment. If these people suffered some sort of trauma, it really does not make any difference whether it was a Ustasha camp or Auschwitz or whether he slipped and fell in front of whatever hospital this doctor practices in. The fact is that he sustained some sort of trauma. That is the statement that would be for medical diagnosis and treatment. Furthermore, he is trying to get in the back door what this Trial Chamber has already said he cannot get in the front door. He is trying to basically lift himself by his own boot straps and it just doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see a couple of problems with what Mr. Ostberg is trying to do right now. I suspect, without knowing for sure, that he has had a conversation with Ms. McHenry and she has told him about an American hearsay exception called "the Business Records Exception" and given him at least some of the steps necessary to establish a business record, although they have not all been given, because there are actually more prongs to that process than have been mentioned so far, including a record made by a person with knowledge at or near the time of receiving the information which has not been established but I think that does not really apply in this Tribunal in any event. We are talking about as a result of the Tadic Decision a pure reliability standard. Now, if we start with document number one that we have been talking about, Mr. Kuljanin, so far to my knowledge there is no evidence before this Tribunal that establishes that this person was at Celebici camp. The question becomes the reliability of this person's statements and its relevance to anything contained in the indictment before this Tribunal. We have no idea, or I have no idea at least, who this person, Novica Kuljanin is. I understand there was a time that the International Committee for the Red Cross came and recorded the names of persons who were confined in Celebici. If this person's name appears on that list, I would think that would be proper evidence that this person was, in fact, in Celebici, but for this document that is being offered to you now to become evidence in this case without some showing of who this person, Novica Kuljanin, is and he is a person whose word we can take, we are just garbaging up the record. The other thing that concerns me is this. If there is that underlying showing of reliability and the documents are only being offered for the name of the person involved and the statements that that person made to the doctor, then I would ask that before they ever become part of this record that every other part of that record be redacted by using an indelible black pen of some form, because there is a danger in the future, either Appellate Chamber or beyond, that someone could conclude that everything contained in these documents is part of the evidence in this case; in other words, if what we are offering is only a portion of the documents, then that is all that ought to wind up in evidence. That does not waive any objection that I have to the whole idea of getting them admitted as a business record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other thing again with reliability. I would point to just the very first one, Mr. Kuljanin. On the front page this document says "X-ray is enclosed." Then I would refer the Trial Chamber to the transcript of today, page 68, line 11: "No X-rays were made in the case of Kuljanin". That goes directly to the reliability. These things flat aren't reliable, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the witness was talking about Mr. Novica Kuljanin, and Mr. Moran has just pointed it out in the transcript, the witness said there were no X-rays with regard to this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This last point I must object to because the witness said he did not have any recognition more than what was in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then I suggest that the Prosecution look at the transcript from today, page 68, lines 11 and 12, which I just read to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Back to the point, if I am allowed to have a word. I can't -- this reduction problem, I do not see before a panel of learned judges and not with a jury that the judges could have any troubles of seeing what in a document is tendered and what is not tendered, and that makes it absolutely clear what I want to do and what I intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, let me find out. What actually are you trying to show in merely admitting a business matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The business and what the persons said, taken down by the doctor without -- as before, starting during medical evaluation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because I do not see a distinction between that fact and just the record, because all you have is the address, for instance, and every other thing contains mainly the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am taking away the opinion. It is what the patient told the doctor, not what the patient found doing this and that using X-rays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the problem. What is the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That these people are coming telling the doctor: "I have this and that pains. I have been detained in the Celebici camp". The relevance is that these are people from Celebici camp telling people that they have come from Celebici camp. That makes it relevant. I am quite prepared to read the portion of it that I would like to tender, if it pleases the court, only the portion what the patient told the doctor. To start again with Mr. Kuljanin, his name is given ..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I still find it difficult to be satisfied with what you are trying to do. It does not help one in any way. It does not, because I do not see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have tried to lay out the relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Sorry. I have tried to demonstrate that I see the relevance is in people from Celebici giving their names, going to the doctor, telling what has happened to them, that that has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, they have not said what happened to them in the camp. Look at the Doctor's opinion. They have been in the camp. Then they were complaining about something. They do not say they received those injuries in the camp. Please refer to any statement where the person examined by the doctor says that: "I received these injuries in the camp." We are concerned with what happened inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So you must show the relevancy then. How is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is the doctor referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Show the relevancy. Read any report you want to bring us on the record anyone who went and told him: "I received these injuries inside." How is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If that is not considered to be implicit in it when it says: "Patient admitted after being released from".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "After being released from." Your own evidence says that these persons before they reached Celebici camp were brutally treated. All the witnesses have said they were beaten up. You must show the relevancy of these observations to the case before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I cannot do that in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These reports do not show that, so how is it relevant? We are concerned with what happened inside the camp. You can get a business record of anyone, but it must have relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then they were examined months after their release. Maybe somebody had a fall. Somebody received his injuries in some other manner. It must be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Obviously, obviously, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Show me any report where any witness has said that he received his injuries inside the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This of course, would be a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are dealing with a criminal case where the benefit of any doubt goes to the accused. You must show me any report that says he received his injuries inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I can do it only in asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what I said. Ask him questions about the witnesses who are going to appear before us. Then that will probably become relevant as supporting evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Meaning then only the witnesses to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because they can come and say they received these injuries inside the camp. You know, the rule of hearsay is subject to two qualifications. It must be relevant and it must have probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Jan. The interpretation booth is waving for you to turn on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All I was saying is the rule of hearsay is subject to two qualifications. One is relevancy and the other is probative value. If the other person is not appearing, then how do we know they received the injuries inside the camp? We have heard evidence that these persons, particularly from Bradina, were brutally treated before they were taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, your Honour, on the face of the statements it certainly says virtually all of them: Celebici, Konjic; Celebici, Konjic, Tarcin; Celebici, Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All they are saying is they were released. Nobody is saying these injuries were received inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are not restricted to Celebici. Some of them deal with other camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Some of them happened in Musala after Celebici. There is evidence that Musala was bombed, was shelled and some people received their injuries there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, as I have said, I am not satisfied with the document having any reference to what you are claiming it does have. I see even no continuity on the document. I see nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What I can do, your Honours, is to ask to go into private session and go through the five names of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Those are witnesses -- those witnesses are not before us yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: One has been before your Honours and I will start with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Pages 3156 to 3167 in closed session
